messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 75
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: QA Engineer
  trauma_type: Natural disaster
  pcl5: 46

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Olfactory (Smoke): Smoke or fire smell, Visual (Fire/Flames): Fire or flames, Weather Similarity: Similar weather conditions to when the event happened
  Maladaptive Strategies: Self-Blame Rumination: I dwell on what I have done wrong, Rumination: Prevention: ruminate about how event could have been prevented, Thought Suppression: I try to push them out of my mind
  Threat: Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard, Startle Response: Feeling jumpy or easily startled

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

At 75, Ernesto Alvarez came to treatment still speaking about the wildfire as if part of him were standing inside it. He is a married Latino man who has spent decades working as a QA engineer, a job he once valued for its orderliness and its emphasis on catching small problems before they became larger ones. The disaster occurred during a period of hot, windy weather when he and his wife were at home. He remembered the first sign as the smell. Smoke had drifted in before he saw anything, a sharp burnt odor that made him pause and go to the window. When he looked out, he saw flames moving in the distance and then, with frightening speed, closer than he had believed possible. The sky had an eerie color, and the weather itself seemed dangerous to him—the dry wind, the heat, the sense that the air was helping the fire along. He has never described the event in dramatic language, but he returns again and again to the same concrete moments: the smell of smoke filling the house, the sight of flames where there should not have been any, and the feeling that the conditions outside had turned familiar surroundings into something hostile.

In the weeks afterward, Ernesto tried to act as though he could put the experience aside if he were disciplined enough. He told himself there was no point dwelling on it, and when images or thoughts came up, he would deliberately force his attention elsewhere. He would turn on the television, start a household task, or move immediately into some practical line of thinking, trying to push the memories out of his mind before they took hold. But the thoughts returned in another form. He found himself sitting for long periods replaying what had happened and asking what he had done wrong. He would go over decisions made that day, wondering whether he should have noticed the danger sooner, whether he should have reacted faster, whether some small action on his part could have changed what happened. Just as often, his mind would move into long, circular efforts to work out how the disaster could have been prevented at all, as if enough analysis might finally produce an answer that would make the event feel less unbearable.

Over the following months, Ernesto became acutely sensitive to reminders in daily life. The smell of smoke was especially potent. If a neighbor used a fireplace, if something scorched on the stove, or if he caught even a faint burnt odor outdoors, his body reacted before he had time to think. He described his heart pounding, his muscles tightening, and a rush of alarm that felt out of proportion to the present moment but completely convincing while it was happening. Seeing flames could do the same. Even ordinary fire—candles on a table, a grill being lit, footage of a house fire on television—could stop him in place. Weather also took on a new meaning. On hot, dry, windy days resembling the conditions of the wildfire, he became watchful and tense, scanning the horizon, checking the air, listening for signs that something might be wrong.

This vigilance followed him into the routines of his life. Ernesto still worked as a QA engineer, and even in that structured environment he found himself distracted by reminders. If he smelled something electrical heating up in the office or saw an image with flames on a screen, his attention narrowed immediately. He would look around, listen, and check for danger, sometimes losing track of the work in front of him. He startled easily as well. A sudden sound in the office or at home could make him jump hard enough to embarrass him, and he had become more aware of how much time he spent braced for something unexpected. His wife noticed that he was less at ease and harder to settle. He did not speak freely about the disaster with her, not because it meant little to him, but because he was trying so hard not to let the thoughts in. Yet the more he tried to clamp down on them, the more often she would find him quiet and preoccupied, staring off as if he were back in that day’s weather.

By the time he sought help, Ernesto was exhausted by the constant state of readiness in his own body and by the relentless mental review of what he should have done differently. What frightened him most was how quickly a simple smell, a flicker of flame, or a certain kind of wind could make him feel that the danger was present again. He had come to believe that he should have been able to prevent something, or at least foresee it, and he could not stop measuring himself against that standard. He was also tired of living as though ordinary sensations were warnings. Coming to treatment, he said he hoped for some relief from the jumpiness and the vigilance, but just as important, he wanted to stop feeling that every reminder pulled him back into the same unanswered question of what he had done wrong.
